entries.clue: Carry on Sir deplorably impounded by pain in the arse (7)

indicatorNotes.deplorably: Something done deplorably is done badly, so the letters of the word before it come out in a wretched order
indicatorNotes.impounded by: What is impounded is shut inside a pound, so these letters end up locked inside the next piece

blocks.note: a pain in the arse is a pest, split around the middle piece as PE…ST
SIR rearranged, sitting in the middle of PEST

annotation.surface: A knighted grandee carrying on so badly that he is being put up with by someone insufferable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carry on Sir' reads like a film title or an order to a knight; the definition is just the first two words. 'Pain in the arse' is Private Eye's bluntness standing in for a plain PEST.
annotation.definitionFit: To persist is to carry on with something despite opposition, a plain synonym.

entries.clue: All together: let's start to penetrate stupid bone head of Cameron! (2,4)

indicatorNotes.start: The start of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letter of "let's" is wanted
indicatorNotes.to penetrate: To penetrate is to push inside, so this letter goes into the middle of the jumbled piece
indicatorNotes.stupid: A stupid arrangement is a senseless one, so the letters of the word that follows are scrambled
indicatorNotes.head of: The head of anything is its top, so just the first letter of the name is taken

blocks.note: BONE rearranged, split as ENB…O around the next letter
the first letter of "let's", pushed inside the scrambled BONE
the first letter of Cameron, added at the end

annotation.surface: A rallying cry for everyone to jab at the thick skull of David Cameron, then Prime Minister.
annotation.walkthrough: The colon makes 'All together' look like a heading for the chant that follows; it is the definition. 'Stupid bone head' sits there as an insult, which hides that 'stupid' works on BONE and 'head' belongs to Cameron.
annotation.definitionFit: En bloc is French borrowed into English for 'as a single group', which is what all together means.

entries.clue: Nigel's last gasp UKIP resort "Right for Independence", which is ignitable (5,4)

annotation.definitionNote: A spark plug is the thing that ignites the fuel rather than the thing that catches, so 'ignitable' stretches the sense to 'to do with igniting'; the setter leans on the word for its surface.

indicatorNotes.last: The last of a name is its final letter, so only the closing letter of Nigel is wanted
indicatorNotes.resort: To resort letters is to sort them all over again, so the whole collection is rearranged
indicatorNotes.for: One thing used for another stands in its place, so the first letter named replaces the second

blocks.note: the final letter of Nigel
the word as written
the party name with its I swapped for R, as the next fragment instructs
R (right) takes the place of I (independence) in UKIP

annotation.surface: Nigel Farage's final desperate UKIP push at a seaside town under a 'Right for Independence' banner, all ready to go up in flames.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Resort' is the trap: next to UKIP and Farage it reads as a seaside town, but it is re-sort, rearrange. R and I are standard shorthand for right and independent, and Independence is just the capitalised slogan form.
annotation.definitionFit: A spark plug is the part in a petrol engine that makes the spark setting the fuel mixture alight.

entries.clue: Bastard whose name can't be remembered (2-3-2)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition is a relative clause describing a person rather than a noun; read it as 'person whose name can't be remembered'.

blocks.note: a euphemism for someone unpleasant, used in place of the ruder word
the same stock phrase is the placeholder for a person whose name escapes the speaker

annotation.surface: An illegitimate child nobody can put a name to.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one description of a nameless foundling. The euphemism is the link: the polite so-and-so replaces 'bastard', and the same words fill in for a forgotten name.
annotation.definitionFit: So-and-so is both a mild stand-in for an insult like bastard and a placeholder for someone whose name you cannot recall.

entries.clue: Balls provided with drug stimulant to achieve an erection? (7)

blocks.note: Ed Balls, Labour's shadow chancellor in 2015
'provided' and 'if' both set a condition
ice is street slang for crystal methamphetamine, a stimulant

annotation.surface: Testicles dosed with a pill to get a man going: the Viagra joke Private Eye cannot resist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Balls' at the start of a sentence hides its capital: it is Ed Balls, the politician. The question mark lets 'an erection' mean a building instead of what the surface wants.
annotation.definitionFit: An erection in its formal sense is anything built or erected, and an edifice is a large building.

entries.clue: Cover up a Spice Girl's spot? (7)

indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry, 'up' sends letters climbing from the bottom, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: a cover is a LID, reversed
Emma Bunton, 'Baby Spice' of the 1990s pop group

annotation.surface: Concealer on a pop star's pimple.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cover up' and 'spot' both pull toward make-up over a blemish. The spot is the tight corner you are in, and the 's means 'is'.
annotation.definitionFit: Being in a spot means being in an awkward situation, and a dilemma is a situation with no good way out.

entries.clue: see 9dn. (5)
Like Campbell's lot, say, causing conflict, holding up boozer (8)

indicatorNotes.holding: Something holding another thing has it inside, so these letters wrap around the next piece
indicatorNotes.up: In a down entry, 'up' sends letters climbing from the bottom, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: to clash is to cause conflict, split as CLA…SH
a boozer is British slang for a pub, an INN, turned round

annotation.surface: Alastair Campbell and his spin team stirring up rows while propping up a bar.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Campbell's lot' sounds like Tony Blair's spin doctor and his crew; 'say' flags the Campbells as one example of a Scottish clan, the family famously at feud with the MacDonalds.
annotation.definitionFit: Clannish describes a group that sticks tightly together, and the Campbells are literally a clan, so they are clannish by example.

entries.clue: (& 7dn.) Concur IMF row loomed over organisation whose chief contribution to global improvement is hot air? (5,8)

annotation.definition: organisation whose chief contribution to global improvement is hot air?

indicatorNotes.over: Something knocked over is upset, so the letters before it tumble into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, all 18 letters

annotation.surface: An International Monetary Fund quarrel hanging over a body that mostly talks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Row loomed over' reads as a news report on the IMF; only 'over' is instruction, the rest is letters. The definition is the Eye's sneer at the annual Davos gathering.
annotation.definitionFit: The World Economic Forum is the organisation behind the Davos summit, and calling its contribution hot air mocks it as a talking shop.

entries.clue: 'Bluster' party introduced by supporter (very American) (7)

indicatorNotes.introduced by: Someone introduced by another comes after them, so the supporter's letters go in front

blocks.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment
the usual abbreviation for very
the usual abbreviation for American
a do is an informal party

annotation.surface: A loud-mouthed party brought forward by one of its backers, very much in the American style.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Supporter' next to 'party' suggests a political backer; here it is the undergarment. The brackets hold two abbreviations, V and A, dropped between the other two pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: Bravado is a show of boldness meant to impress, much the same thing as bluster.

entries.clue: Cowboy's dangly thing produced a trial (6)

indicatorNotes.produced: Something produced has been made up out of materials, so the letters of the phrase are made into a new word

blocks.note: anagram fodder, six letters

annotation.surface: A cowboy's private parts turned out to be evidence in a court case.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dangly thing' pushes the Eye's usual smut, but the cowboy's dangly thing hangs from his saddle.
annotation.definitionFit: A lariat is a cowboy's lasso, the looped rope he carries hanging at his side.

entries.clue: (& 14ac.) Labour free to come undone? (4)

blocks.note: labour is work
set free is let loose

annotation.surface: Wondering whether the Labour Party, left to itself, would fall apart.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital L turns 'Labour' into the party, but it is plain toil. The question mark admits that free labour coming undone is the surface's political jab.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that works loose gradually comes free of its fixing, which is coming undone.

entries.clue: see 12ac. (5)
Ex-president's after a lead from Monica to "jump" (6)

indicatorNotes.'s after: Coming after something puts it later in the line, so the president's name follows the other pieces
indicatorNotes.lead from: A lead is what goes in front, so the first letter of the name is taken

blocks.note: the word as written
the first letter of Monica
George Bush, either of the two former US presidents

annotation.surface: A former president going after a lead from Monica Lewinsky for a quick leap into bed.
annotation.walkthrough: Monica Lewinsky belongs to Clinton, which makes a solver reach for him; the ex-president wanted is Bush. The quoted 'jump' is the attack sense, not the leap.
annotation.definitionFit: To jump someone is slang for attacking them without warning, which is to ambush them.

entries.clue: Genesis augmented by Thatcher for a spot (9)

indicatorNotes.augmented by: Something augmented has extra added onto it, so the second piece is tacked on the end of the first

blocks.note: a genesis is a birth or beginning
Mark Thatcher, Margaret Thatcher's son

annotation.surface: The Book of Genesis padded out by Mrs Thatcher to fill a slot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thatcher' sounds like Margaret; the name wanted is her son, Mark. Genesis is the beginning, not the book or the band.
annotation.definitionFit: A birthmark is a coloured patch on the skin present from birth, a kind of spot.

entries.clue: Green fiasco – storing cool energy for Telford, maybe (8)

indicatorNotes.fiasco: A fiasco is a mess, so the word before it is left in a jumbled state
indicatorNotes.storing: Something storing things keeps them inside, so these letters take in the next piece

blocks.note: GREEN rearranged, split as ENG…ER
in is slang for fashionable, cool
the physicist's symbol for energy

annotation.surface: An environmentalist disaster over saving cool, clean energy for the Shropshire new town of Telford.
annotation.walkthrough: Telford is a Shropshire new town, which fits the energy-policy surface, but it is named after Thomas Telford. 'Green' sits as a policy word when it is only the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Thomas Telford was a Scottish civil engineer who built roads, canals and bridges, so he is one example of an engineer.

entries.clue: Board member makes £1000 by day's end (6)

indicatorNotes.by: One thing by another stands next to it, so the thousand sits right beside the second piece

blocks.note: K is short for a thousand, as in a £40K salary
night is what the day ends in

annotation.surface: A company director taking home a grand a day.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Board member' suggests a company director drawing fees; the board is a chessboard. 'Day's end' is a whole word, not a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A knight is one of the pieces on a chessboard, so a board member in the game sense.

entries.clue: Parliament takes nothing from volatile Lady T, now (7)

indicatorNotes.takes: To take one thing from another is to remove it, so a letter comes out of the phrase
indicatorNotes.from: What is taken from something is subtracted out of it, so the letter comes away from the phrase that follows
indicatorNotes.volatile: A volatile thing is unstable, so the remaining letters will not stay in the order given

blocks.note: nothing is O, the letter removed from NOW
the letters of LADY T NOW without the O, then rearranged

annotation.surface: The House of Commons taking nothing from an unpredictable Margaret Thatcher, now.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lady T' was the tabloids' name for Margaret Thatcher, which makes Westminster the obvious parliament. This one is the Isle of Man's.
annotation.definitionFit: Tynwald is the parliament of the Isle of Man, the Crown dependency in the Irish Sea.

entries.clue: (& 25ac.) Partner screws for health (5)

indicatorNotes.screws: To screw something up is to twist and crumple it, so the letters that follow are twisted out of shape

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

annotation.surface: A spouse having sex for the good of their health.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Screws' is Private Eye's crude verb in the surface and a twisting instruction in the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Your other half is an informal British phrase for your spouse or partner.

entries.clue: Vatican: "Break Eye's resolution!" (4,3)

indicatorNotes.resolution: Resolving something breaks it down into its parts and works them into shape, so the letters are reworked into a new order

blocks.note: hols, short for holidays, are a break from work
the magazine's name with the possessive 's dropped, leaving its three letters for the mix

annotation.surface: The Vatican ordering Private Eye to break its New Year's resolution.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Break' looks like the command in the Pope's order; it is a noun, a break, as in a holiday. Put that with Eye and rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: The Holy See is the Pope's jurisdiction as a sovereign entity, run from the Vatican, so the two names stand for each other.

entries.clue: Become bloody thick male, and get in the habit (6)

blocks.note: blood that thickens clots
he is the male pronoun

annotation.surface: A stupid bloke turning into an idiot and settling into a routine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bloody thick male' reads as a string of insults for a bloke. The habit is a monk's or nun's robe.
annotation.definitionFit: To clothe someone is to dress them, and getting into a habit is putting on a monk's or nun's robe.

entries.clue: Description of Necker Island? It's quite uncultivated (6,4)

blocks.note: Necker Island is owned by Richard Branson, founder of the Virgin group, so its ground belongs to his brand
land that has never been ploughed or farmed

annotation.surface: A travel note on Branson's private Caribbean island, saying its ground is barely farmed.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital V is the hidden joke: the first reading wants Branson's company, the second the ordinary adjective. The question mark marks the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: Virgin soil means ground that has never been cultivated, and Necker, being Branson's, is soil owned by Virgin.

entries.clue: Hague's second houses speculation (5)

indicatorNotes.houses: Something that houses a thing holds it inside, so the answer is sitting within the words before it

blocks.note: haGUE'S Second

annotation.walkthrough: 'Second houses' pairs up as holiday homes, and 'Hague's second' as a letter; neither is the reading. The answer runs across the apostrophe in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: A guess is an opinion formed without proof, the same thing as a speculation.

entries.clue: see 20ac. (4)

annotation.definition: As you'd expect from a Russell Brand appearance

indicatorNotes.untrammelled outburst: An outburst bursts out in no order, and untrammelled means with nothing holding it back, so the letters break free into a new arrangement

V for victory, buried among the rest

annotation.surface: Russell Brand on stage letting fly with one of his rants.

indicatorNotes.entrance: An entrance is the way in, so only the first letter of Tony is taken
indicatorNotes.outlandish: Outlandish means strange and foreign, so all the gathered letters are put into an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation for new
the first letter of Tony
the word as written

annotation.walkthrough: 'New' and Tony point to New Labour and Tony Blair, and Mo to Mo Mowlam of his cabinet. Here Mo is just short for moment.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Half a mo' is British slang for a moment, and an instant is a moment.

entries.clue: Like making a retreat in offensive holy war (7)

indicatorNotes.making a retreat: An army making a retreat goes back the way it came, so this word runs backwards
indicatorNotes.in: One thing in another sits inside it, so the reversed word goes into the middle of the next

entries.clue: Bloody hell, the French! They're a nuisance vote-seeking politicians have to deal with (7)

annotation.definition: They're a nuisance vote-seeking politicians have to deal with

blocks.note: heck is the mild stand-in for hell
les is French for 'the' before a plural noun

annotation.surface: A British politician swearing at the French, pictured as a nuisance to deal with.
